scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

prediction.raw: This is a complex and emotionally charged situation, and there’s no simple "right" or "wrong" answer—it depends on perspective, values, and the context of your relationship with your father. However, I’ll break it down objectively to help you reflect on the ethical and relational dimensions of your actions. ### **Ethical Perspective (AITA?)** **Score: ~0.3 (Neutral-Leaning "No")** Here’s why: 1. **Ownership & Consent**: - Your father *did* share the idea with you, but he never explicitly granted you the right to take it and commercialize it without his involvement or consent. Even if he didn’t "formally" assign you ownership, he had a reasonable expectation that the idea would stay within the family or be developed *with* him. - Stealing intellectual property—even from a family member—is ethically questionable because it violates trust and the principle of **fairness**. If you had asked him to partner with you, he might have agreed (or not), but taking it without discussion is exploitative. 2. **Exploitation of His Strengths**: - You acknowledged that your father is brilliant but lacks execution skills. While you’re right that he’s not a "man of action," that doesn’t give you the right to bypass him entirely. His idea was his contribution, and your success built on it should have included him in some capacity—even if just as a silent partner or advisor. - Your comment, *"You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action,"* is dismissive. It implies his value is only in brainstorming, not in the final outcome. That’s unfair. 3. **The Offer of 20% Profits**: - While generous, this was a **last-minute gesture** after the fact. A fair approach would have been to discuss ownership *before* launching the business. Even then, 20% is low—if he was the original idea holder, he should have had a significant stake (e.g., 30-50%). 4. **Emotional Impact**: - Your father’s reaction—feeling betrayed and nearly crying—is valid. You’ve taken something he considered his, turned it into success, and then offered him crumbs. That’s not just unethical; it’s emotionally harmful. - Your mother and grandfather taking your side suggests a **generational divide** (you vs. your father), but that doesn’t excuse the action. Family loyalty doesn’t override moral principles. --- ### **Relational Perspective (Why He’s Upset)** Your father’s reaction isn’t just about the business—it’s about **trust, respect, and legacy**: - **Betrayal**: He shared an idea he cared about with you, expecting it to be handled with care. Instead, you took it and made it yours. - **Unfair Advantage**: You used his intellectual property to build something successful while excluding him. That feels like he was **used** rather than respected. - **Generational Conflict**: You framed this as a "traditional masculine" vs. "modern" dynamic, but that’s not the issue. The issue is **how you treated him**. Even if he’s "not a man of action," he still deserves dignity in his contributions. --- ### **What Should You Have Done?** 1. **Ask for Permission First**: - If you wanted to pursue the idea, you should have said, *"Dad, I love this idea. Can I help develop it with you?"* or *"Should I take it and run with it?"* His answer would have been his choice. 2. **Offer a Fair Deal**: - If you decided to go alone, you should have offered him **equity, mentorship, or a revenue share** upfront—not as an afterthought. 3. **Acknowledge His Role**: - Even if he didn’t "get things done," he was the **source of the idea**. You can’t take credit for that without acknowledging his contribution. 4. **Apologize & Rebuild Trust**: - Right now, you’re in a defensive position. A genuine apology (without excuses) could go a long way. Example: *"I realize now that taking your idea without discussing it first was wrong. I should have asked you first. I’m sorry for hurting you. Can we find a way to move forward that feels fair to both of us?"* --- ### **Final Verdict: Was It Right?** **No, it was not right.** Stealing an idea—even from a family member—is unethical, and your father’s reaction is justified. That said, **you can still fix it** by: - Taking responsibility. - Offering a **better deal** (e.g., 30-50% equity, a consulting role, or a one-time payment). - Showing humility and a willingness to rebuild trust. If you truly want to repair the relationship, **action > words**. Words alone won’t undo the hurt you’ve caused. Would you like help drafting a message to your father to start the conversation?
